summary: Defines a YANG data model for key chains, lists of keys with IDs, send and accept lifetimes, and algorithms. They are used for routing protocol authentication. Overlapping lifetimes allow keys to be changed gracefully, and a data model enables automated key distribution.

eli5.summary: A key ring where each key works only during certain dates, so you can swap old for new without a gap.

questions: what is a yang key chain
how does graceful key rollover work
how are key chain keys protected
subtitle: A standard YANG model for key chains, so routers can hold keys with lifetimes and swap them without breaking authentication.

tldr.problem: Network devices use lists of keys to authenticate routing protocols, but each vendor configures them differently, which makes automated key distribution and smooth key changes harder.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines the ietf-key-chain YANG module: named key chains containing keys, each with a Key ID, key string, cryptographic algorithm and send and accept lifetimes that can overlap.
tldr.outcome: Other YANG modules can reference a key chain by name, and keys can be changed gracefully by overlapping lifetimes. The module is designed to be reached through NETCONF or RESTCONF.

today: RFC 8177 is a Proposed Standard published in June 2017, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. Its module is meant to be extended by vendors and referenced by other YANG modules.

sections.title: What a Key Chain Is
sections.content:
A key chain is a list of one or more elements. Each element holds a Key ID, a key string, send and accept lifetimes, and the authentication or encryption algorithm to use. Key chains are commonly used for routing protocol authentication and other applications that need symmetric keys. This RFC describes them as a YANG data model.

By overlapping the send and accept lifetimes of several elements, key strings and algorithms can be updated gracefully. Because the keys live in a YANG model, distribution can be automated. In some applications, such as the master keys of TCP-AO, the protocol does not use the key directly but derives a short-lived key from it.
sections.eli5: A key chain is a ring of keys, and each key comes with a label saying what it does and when it works.

sections.title: The Problem and Graceful Rollover
sections.content:
The RFC says key chains have been implemented and deployed by a large percentage of network equipment vendors. A standard YANG model should ease automated key distribution and non-disruptive key rollover, supporting the tightening of core routing security recommended in RFC 4948. A key chain is described as a reusable key policy that can be referenced wherever needed. It differs from the crypto key table in RFC 7210, which has key selection criteria. This model has none, but does not preclude them.

For graceful key rollover, a receiver MAY accept every key whose accept lifetime is valid, while the sender MAY use the key with the most recent send lifetime. The suggested steps are:

  • Distribute a key chain with the new key to all devices. Its accept lifetime covers the rollover period, and its send lifetime starts in the future.
  • Make sure every device is updated and that system times are roughly synchronized, for example using NTP.
  • When the new key's send lifetime begins, devices start sending with it.
  • Later, optionally distribute a chain without the old key. This may wait until the next rollover.

The most recent send lifetime is the one with the latest start time, so a send lifetime of always prevents this technique.
sections.eli5: To switch keys, first hand out the new key so everyone can recognize it. Only later, on a set day, does everyone start using it. Nobody gets locked out during the switch.

sections.title: Design of the Key Chain Model
sections.content:
The ietf-key-chain module holds one or more keys indexed by key-id. For some applications, such as OSPFv3, the Key ID selects which key to use. Each key also has a key string and a cryptographic algorithm, and optionally send and accept lifetimes. If no lifetime is given, the key is always valid. A key chain has a name unique within the device, and other modules SHOULD use the key-chain-ref typedef to reference it.

Different values for sending and accepting can be set with multiple elements. A sending key has a valid send lifetime and an invalid accept lifetime, for instance an end time equal to its start time. An accepting key is the reverse. A lifetime can be always, or a start time followed by an infinite end, a duration in seconds, or an end time. With the independent-send-accept-lifetime feature a key has separate send and accept lifetimes.

Operational state shares the tree with configuration, in line with the Network Management Datastore Architecture. It includes the last modification timestamp and read-only flags, send-lifetime-active and accept-lifetime-active, showing whether each key is valid now. The key string can be plain text or, with the hex-key-string feature, hexadecimal.
sections.eli5: Each key card has a number, a secret word, a scrambling method, and dates for using it. A card with no dates works all the time.

sections.title: Features and Algorithms
sections.content:
Vendors differ, so optional parts are YANG features. They cover differences in what vendors support, such as an acceptance tolerance or hexadecimal key strings. They also cover security requirements not yet implemented by every vendor, such as TCP-AO algorithms.

The module defines algorithm identities that can be reused when configuring legacy authentication or encryption that does not use key chains. They include md5, sha-1, hmac-sha-1, hmac-sha-256, hmac-sha-384 and hmac-sha-512. Feature-gated identities include hmac-sha-1-12, aes-cmac-prf-128, cleartext and replay-protection-only. The last provides replay protection without authentication, as needed by protocols such as BFD.
sections.eli5: Not every device knows every trick, so extras are optional add-ons. The list of scrambling methods is shared so other tools can pick from the same menu.

sections.title: Protecting the Keys
sections.content:
The module is meant to be accessed through network management protocols like NETCONF or RESTCONF. NETCONF's mandatory secure transport is SSH, and RESTCONF's is TLS. The key strings are not accessible by default, and NETCONF access control model rules are required to configure or retrieve them.

Key strings can be encrypted with AES Key Wrap. The key-encryption key is not in the model and must be set or derived separately. This requires the hex-key-string feature too. The RFC RECOMMENDS this encryption to avoid retrieving and storing key chains with keys in cleartext, independent of access control.

The cleartext algorithm is NOT RECOMMENDED except where nothing else works, for instance a legacy device that must authenticate BFD packets at intervals of 10 milliseconds or less for many peers. Those keys SHOULD NOT be reused with more secure algorithms. MD5 and SHA-1 are also described as insecure and NOT RECOMMENDED, except for backward compatibility.
sections.eli5: The key ring is kept in a locked box, and you can wrap each key in a second lock. Using keys written in plain view is a last resort.

sections.title: Examples and IANA
sections.content:
Appendix A gives NETCONF examples: a chain with one always-valid key, a chain whose keys have different lifetimes, and a chain with independent send and accept lifetimes.

IANA registered the XML namespace urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:yang:ietf-key-chain and the YANG module named ietf-key-chain, with the prefix key-chain.
sections.eli5: The appendix shows sample key rings, and the module got its official name in a public list.
